newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to pursue landmine ban via Geneva conference.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to pursue landmine ban via Geneva conference.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it will unilaterally observe a permanent ban on the export of anti-personnel landmines and seek a global ban via the Conference on Disarmament that starts on Monday in Geneva.

The U.S. decision to pursue a ban through Geneva appears to be a blow to Canada's efforts to negotiate a ban through its "Ottawa process" of talks, which two key countries -- Russia and China -- say they will not support.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry made the announcements in his daily briefing, saying that President Bill Clinton had also decided the United States would cap its stockpile of such landmines at its existing level of several million.
The ban would apply only to anti-personnel landmines, which are designed to injure people, rather than anti-armour mines, which are made to destroy heavy vehicles like tanks.

"When the Conference on Disarmament opens ... in Geneva on Monday the United States will seek to initiate negotiations on a worldwide treaty banning the use, production, stockpiling and transfer of anti-personnel landmines," McCurry said.

U.S. officials said the decision to pursue the matter in Geneva, rather than through the Ottawa process, reflected the conclusion that Geneva would be a more effective forum, not least of all because Russia and China would attend.

Russia and China are seen as the primary global suppliers of landmines, more than 100 million of which lie buried or hidden in 64 countries around the world. Some 25,000 people a year are killed or maimed by mines left when wars end.
The Conference on Disarmament, which operates under the aegis of the United Nations, is a universal forum where countries meet periodically to discuss disarmament.

"In order for this to be an effective ban, it needs to be univeral or virtually so," said a U.S. official who asked not to be named. "We believe ... we should concentrate our effort on a negotiating forum where it is most likely to be universal."
Sarah Walkling, senior analyst with the Washington-based Arms Control Association, suggested that without Russia and China, Canada's effort may be more symbolic than substantive.

"If it's not going to be much more than a paper tiger, which is what the Ottowa process is beginning to look like, then what's the point?," said Walkling, whose group has not taken a formal stance on the matter.

The White House's decision to unilaterally observe a ban on the export and transfer of anti-personnel landmines extends an existing, temporary ban put in place under legislation sponsored by Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat.

Last May Clinton ordered more than four million so-called "dumb" anti-personnel landmines removed from U.S. arsenals and destroyed. However he said Washington would keep those mines it currently has in South Korea.
"Dumb" landmines are those that do not self destruct.

U.S. officials told reporters at the Pentagon the United States currently had one million older anti-personnel mines sown in South Korea and an additional three million such "dumb" mines in its stockpile. That stockpile is being destroyed and so far 300,000 have been rendered harmless.
They said the United States also has anti-personnel mines in use at the Navy's Guantanamo Bay base in Cuba, where 12,000 mines are being gathered and destroyed.

They said the military also has "several million" newer self-destructing anti-personnel mines in its inventory and that Washington reserves the right to use them until a global ban is agreed upon or military alternatives are found.
